definition: Insatiable means incapable of being satisfied.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word insatiable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know insatiable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: No matter how many thrillers the library buys, Mr. Okafor's insatiable reading appetite clears the new-arrivals shelf by Friday.
Eager wants keenly and waits politely; insatiable wants without end — feeding it only sharpens it.
Ravenous is hunger at full roar, but even a ravenous crew is quiet after two pots of stew; insatiable outlasts every serving you bring.

Unquenchable is the word for thirsts — no drink puts one out, whether the thirst is for water, for fame, or for knowledge. Insatiable does the same endless work for hunger and appetite of every kind: where unquenchable pictures the fire no water reaches, insatiable names the hunger no meal ends.

Voracious is appetite at enormous scale — a voracious reader devours a shelf a week, a voracious fire eats a hillside. But scale is not endlessness: give the voracious enough, and they finish. Insatiable erases the finish line; no amount, however huge, ever ends the wanting.

Insatiable means incapable of being satisfied.
No matter how many thrillers the library buys, Mr.
Okafor's insatiable reading appetite clears the new-arrivals shelf by Friday.
Forty years in, the map collector's hunger is unchanged: each new atlas satisfies him for exactly one evening.
By breakfast the wanting is back, pointing at a gap on the shelf only he can see.
His spouse stopped asking 'how many is enough?' decades ago — an appetite this insatiable has no number.
Insatiable is built to say exactly this: in- (not) + satis (enough) — no amount is ever enough.
A big appetite can be met with a big meal, and a vast collection can, given years enough, be finished.
Insatiable removes the finish line altogether; the wanting always outlives the getting.
Insatiable describes the hunger, not the meal — curiosity, drive, an audience's demand — and insists no amount will end it.
Gluttony, its unit-mate, judges the behavior at the table: indulging past fullness.
A glutton overshoots 'enough'; the insatiable never meet it.
Keep the vice with the food and insatiable with the endless wanting.

In 1841, readers on two continents were following the fate of Little Nell, the frail heroine of Charles Dickens's serialized novel The Old Curiosity Shop.
Dickens published the story in weekly parts, and the public's appetite for them proved insatiable: each new installment seemed only to sharpen the demand for the next.
Printers ran the presses through the night and still sold out by morning.

When the ship carrying the final chapters neared New York, six thousand people crowded the docks, shouting to the sailors at the rail: 'Is Little Nell dead?' Booksellers had never seen anything like it -- a hunger that sixty installments had fed and fed without once filling.
